concepts.hook: *Tekma*, the fulmar that spits oil from its gut at anyone who comes near its ledge, hangs over the Reach to warn climbers off the cliffs.
*Sirav*, the eider hen who plucks her own breast to line a nest not yet built, rises as a sign of a woman who gives her warmth before she is asked.
*Haku*, the gannet that folds its wings and drops like a thrown gaff into the sea, is the star a boy takes when he dives for a girl's favour and comes up with only salt.
*Halun*, the puffin with a row of sand-eels crossways in its beak, is the star of the provider and of the father who comes home with his mouth full and says nothing.
*Ireth*, the arctic tern that flies pole to pole and back each year, is the star of the lost who turn up late, wet and unembarrassed, after the village has already grieved.
*Skeru*, the raven that sits on the highest stake and puts questions to the wind, is the star of old women who ask the weather too much and are answered.
*Mora*, the ptarmigan that turns white in winter and brown in summer, is hung over the Reach as a joke against people who change their coats with the season.
*Vanu*, the great skua that robs the gulls of their fish low over the water, is the star of borrowed things that are never given back and of the Gulls' long complaint.
*Nethe*, the shag that stands on the rock with its wings spread to dry, always a little too damp, is the star for wet-weather people and for those who wait for better days.
*Kessal*, the oystercatcher with its red blade of a bill prising mussels off the rock, is the star of patient hands and of work done without thanks.
*Lumma*, the male lumpfish who guards his eggs in a crevice until they hatch, is the star of men who sit by the hearth all winter while the boats go out.
*Sekar*, the narwhal with its spear of tusk, is flown by the young who want to go far north and by the old who say the tusk is only a tooth that got ideas.
*Remu*, the grey seal whose song under the ice is heard by drowned sailors' widows, is the star of those who listen at night for a sound that never comes.
*Mulka*, the orca pod whose black fins stand up like sails, is flown at the launch of a new boat so the sea will see it coming and be polite.
*Tirrun*, the herring shoal that turns all at once like a cloth shaken in the wind, is the star of the net-mender's art, of many hands moving as one.
*Hallu*, the split cod hung on the racks, stiff as laths and white with salt, is the star of winter stores and of patience with food that has already died.
*Thisa*, the sea-thrift that flowers in a crack of the cliff where nothing should grow, is the star of the stubborn and of children born on the ledge.
*Vular*, the bladderwrack whose air-bladders rattle when the wave goes over, is the star that tells fishers the tide has turned by sound alone.
*Kanthe*, the angelica kept green for winter, is the star of the medicine-woman's cupboard and of old quarrels smoothed over with a spoonful of seal fat.
*Mektu*, the crowberry with its black fruit on creeping hands, is the star of those who picked too far from home and came back with purple fingers and a lie.
*Sulin*, the cotton-grass that burns white on the bog at dusk, is the star of wet cloth hung out to dry and of the Unflown's joke at anyone who walks toward it.
*Hanthe*, the rowan with its red berries hung over doors against the sea-witch, is the star of protection and of whoever keeps the door open in a gale.
*Kovar*, a grey mare who gallops over the sea throwing ice, whose hooves are the lost stones of the shore, is flown on the first hard day of winter.
*Harlu*, a low wet dog that runs the shore snapping at the heels of anyone out too late, is the star of the one who goes out in the dark to look for a lost boat.
*Ruvem*, who sits on boats and freezes the rope, sail and oar until they are stiff as bone, is flown by widows and by all who keep a cold house.
*Moseth*, a grey heavy ewe that leads lost lambs home through the mist by calling, is the star of whoever finds the way when no one else can see it.
*Skalla*, an old woman in the kelp who pulls rope and hair from drowned boats, is the star of the thing that keeps what the sea gives back and asks a hand in return.
*Torum*, a small grey man who counts the seabird eggs in the sea-caves and lets none leave, is Hesk's counter in the north, and children are told to count their fingers before bed.
*Lesk*, born of a gust that broke in two, runs bucking across the Reach with no mother in sight, and is flown by children who want to show they can run wild.
*Kithru*, the snow buntings that come with the first snow and leave before the thaw, is the star of a first kiss in a hard year and of a promise made in the last light.
